title: The Country We Have Not Seen
subtitle: A five-session study on heaven, hell, and the life to come, and the hope that produces courage instead of escape.
summary:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and individuals who have grown tired of a hope that sounds like clouds and harps and have begun to suspect that the Bible promises something larger, stranger, and far more solid. It walks slowly through five movements on the last things. It clears away the wrong picture of heaven and recovers the biblical hope. It follows N.T. Wright into the resurrection of the body and the redemption of the new earth, what he calls life after life-after-death. It faces hell honestly, laying the historic view of eternal conscious punishment, the conditionalist view, and the reach of universalism each at full strength, without flinching and without gloating. It sits with the intermediate state and the communion of saints, holding grief and hope together at the graveside. And it ends where the whole faith ends, with how the morning that is coming shapes the long defeat we are living now. It is built to be run by a busy volunteer with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than advice.

This is not a study that hands frightened people easy certainties or uses hell as a whip. It will not do that, and the leader must never let it. James Bell came to faith out of atheism, and the doctrine of hell was the thing he held hardest against God, so he does not pretend it is comfortable now. He takes the objection at full weight because he once made it himself. And he does not stand outside any of this. He was raised without a father and has buried people he loved, and he has felt the particular ache of grieving a presence he barely had. He has wanted to flee a world that breaks his heart, and he has wanted to give up the horizon and call it wisdom. He writes from inside the longing and the doubt and the grief. So will you.
audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

sessions.title: The Wrong Picture
sessions.aim: To clear away the clouds-and-harps fantasy that almost everyone, including most Christians, mistakes for heaven, and to recover the biblical hope of a redeemed creation rather than an escape from it.
sessions.summary: Ask a room what heaven is and you will get clouds, harps, robes, and a vague forever of floating somewhere up there, disembodied. That is the picture nearly everyone carries, and it is not the Bible's. The first question is not how to get there but what it even is. Bell, a former atheist, grants the unbeliever the strong form of the complaint, that the popular Christian heaven is both unbelievable and unappealing, a thin bribe of religious tedium. On the popular picture, he says, the critic is mostly right, and the church has defended a counterfeit and then wondered why no one wanted it. He traces the error to Plato, not Scripture, the old lie that the body is a prison and salvation means the soul shedding the flesh. Against it he sets the empty tomb and a physical Jesus who ate fish to prove he was not a ghost. The Christian hope is not the flight of the soul into the sky. It is resurrection, new heavens and a new earth, God coming down to dwell with people, the New Jerusalem descending. Then the turn. The picture you hold of the end shapes the whole of how you live the middle. If heaven is escape, this world is a waiting room and your body a rented suit. If heaven is the redemption of all of it, then nothing good is finally wasted, and we can love this world without clinging to it. We have been handing each other postcards of the wrong place.

keyScripture.why: The last vision in the Bible is not human beings flying up to God but the holy city coming down, the dwelling of God with man, naming the Christian hope as God making his home on a renewed earth rather than souls escaping it.

discussion.q: Before tonight, when you pictured heaven, what did you actually see, clouds and harps, a family reunion, a bright nothing, and where did that picture come from?
discussion.behind: Surface the inherited image before correcting anything. Most people have never examined the picture they carry, and it usually came from paintings, funerals, and hymns rather than Scripture. The aim is to expose the source, gently, so the room can ask whether the picture is even biblical. Go first if it is slow.

discussion.q: Bell, a former atheist, says that on the popular picture the skeptic is mostly right to find heaven unappealing. Why might a sky-bound, disembodied forever be a hope worth disbelieving?
discussion.behind: Let the room feel the force of the objection rather than rushing to defend. The point is to admit the counterfeit deserves the doubt it gets, which clears the ground for the real hope. Do not let anyone resolve it too fast. The honesty here is what makes the recovery credible.

discussion.q: The idea that the body is a prison the soul escapes is Plato, not the Bible. Where have you absorbed the assumption that the point of salvation is to get your soul out of here?
discussion.behind: Help the room notice how deep the Platonic instinct runs in common Christian speech, the released soul, the better place, free of that body at last. The aim is recognition, not shame, that we have baptized an idea Scripture never taught and let it shape how we hope and grieve.

discussion.q: The first evidence for the Christian hope is an empty tomb and a Jesus who ate fish to prove he was not a ghost. What does it change that the hope begins with a raised body and not a freed soul?
discussion.behind: Move the room to the physical center of the faith. A soul-only heaven needs no resurrection, so the empty tomb is the clue that the hope is bodily. Help them feel that whatever heaven is, it is the body's vindication and not its abandonment, which reframes everything that follows in the study.

discussion.q: Bell says the picture you hold of the end shapes how you live the middle. If heaven is escape, this world is a waiting room. How has your picture of the end shaped how you treat this world, your body, your work, the beauty around you?
discussion.behind: Close on the stakes, with self-implication. The aim is to connect the doctrine to daily life, that a too-small hope makes us careless with the world God means to redeem. Invite honest reflection on what an escape-hope has cost us, and go first. The point is reorientation, not a tidy answer.

objections.objection: The Christian heaven is obviously a fairy tale for people too scared of death to accept the end. Clouds, harps, angels, a forever of singing. It is wishful thinking dressed as faith, and no thinking adult should fall for it.
objections.response: Bell grants more of this than you expect, because he made the argument himself as an unbeliever. The clouds-and-harps heaven is a fairy tale, and it deserves to be disbelieved. It is a sub-Christian fantasy stitched from Renaissance paintings and funeral sentiment, and the church has defended the counterfeit and then acted wounded when no one wanted it. Then make the turn. The thing you are rejecting is not actually the Christian hope, it is a fragment mistaken for the whole. The Bible does not promise souls floating in the sky. It promises resurrection, bodies raised on a healed earth, God coming down to dwell among people. You have been right to reject the postcard. Now look at the country it was a bad picture of, and reject that on its own terms if you still can, but at least reject the real thing and not the cartoon.

objections.objection: Does it really matter whether I picture heaven as floating souls or resurrected bodies on a new earth? Either way I get to be with God forever, so why argue over the furniture?
objections.response: It matters more than almost anything, because the picture of the end shapes the whole of the present. If heaven is escape, then this world is a waiting room you are killing time in, your body is a rented suit you will be glad to take off, and the work and the marriage and the aching beauty of an ordinary afternoon are scaffolding to be torn down. People who believe that become careless with the very world God means to redeem. But if the new earth is this earth healed, then the cup of cold water counts, the garden you planted matters, the body you have learned to forgive will be raised, and nothing good is finally wasted. It is not furniture. It is the difference between a faith that flees the world and one that rolls up its sleeves in it.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What is the loss you most quietly fear is final, the person or the place or the part of yourself you cannot imagine being given back, and what would it mean to believe it is not lost but waiting?
sessions.practice: This week, catch yourself every time you use the language of escape about death, gone to a better place, free of that body, an angel now, looking down on us. Do not correct anyone out loud. Just notice, and each time, silently replace it with the larger hope. Not gone, but ahead. Not freed from the body, but waiting for a better one. Not up and away, but held until the morning. Write down what you noticed and whether the larger hope felt truer or only stranger.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, we have pictured the home you are preparing as a thin and bloodless place, and then half believed our own small picture, and grieved as though the grave were the end of the body forever. Forgive us for trading your promise of a healed creation for a postcard of clouds. You made matter and called it good, you became matter and did not stop, you raised your Son in a body that ate and could be touched. Teach us to hope the way the empty tomb teaches us to hope, for resurrection, for a new earth, for your dwelling come down among us. We have not seen that country. Make us long for the real one. Amen.
reflection: Where did my picture of heaven actually come from, and have I ever tested it against what Scripture says rather than what funerals and paintings taught me?
What does it stir in me that the Christian hope is more physical, not less, than I assumed, a raised body on a healed earth rather than a freed soul in the sky?
If this world is going to be redeemed and not discarded, what am I treating as disposable that God means to heal?
sessions.teaching: Begin with the picture, because almost everyone has one, and almost everyone has it wrong. Ask a roomful of people what heaven is and you will get clouds. You will get harps. You will get robes and gates and a vague forever of floating somewhere up there, disembodied, vaguely bored, singing songs that never end in a service that never lets out. That is the picture. And it is not the Bible's. I say this as a man who came to faith out of atheism, so let me tell you what the atheist sees, because I was him. The atheist looks at the Christian heaven and finds it both unbelievable and unappealing, a bribe for the gullible and a thin one at that, an eternity of religious tedium offered to people too frightened of the dark to want anything better. And the church needs to hear this from its critics. On the popular picture, the atheist is mostly right. The clouds-and-harps heaven deserves to be disbelieved. It is a sub-Christian fantasy stitched together from Renaissance paintings and funeral-home sentiment and bad hymns, and it has almost nothing to do with what Scripture actually promises. We have defended a counterfeit and then wondered why no one wanted it. So clear the ground. Heaven, in the popular sense of a disembodied soul drifting in the sky forever, is not the Christian hope. Not even close. It is a fragment of the hope, mistaken for the whole, and the fragment has swallowed the thing it was only ever a part of. What the Bible promises is not escape from the world. It is the rescue and remaking of the world. N.T. Wright has spent a career trying to wake the church from this particular sleep, and his book Surprised by Hope names the confusion precisely. The Christian hope is not that we go up to heaven when we die and stay there as ghosts. It is resurrection. It is new heavens and a new earth. It is bodies, raised and glorified, on a renewed creation, with the dwelling of God come down to be among them. The last image in the Bible is not human beings flying away to God. It is God coming down to dwell with human beings, the New Jerusalem descending, the home of God with man. The movement is downward and earthward, not upward and away. Why did we get it so wrong. Part of the answer is old, and it is not even Christian. It is Plato. The idea that the body is a prison and the soul a trapped spark longing to be free, that matter is low and spirit is high, that salvation means the soul shedding the flesh like a snake leaving its skin, is Greek, not Hebrew. It seeped into the church early and never fully left. We baptized Plato and called him an apostle. And so we came to imagine that the point of the gospel was to get our souls out of here, when the gospel from Genesis to Revelation insists that here, this creation, this world of dirt and bodies and rivers and bread, is exactly what God means to redeem. God made matter. God called it good. God became matter, in the womb of a girl in Nazareth, and did not stop being matter when he rose, because the tomb was empty and the body was gone. Sit with that. The first proof of the Christian hope is an empty tomb and a physical Jesus who ate fish in front of his friends to prove he was not a ghost. If the hope were the flight of the soul, the resurrection of the body is a strange and pointless thing for God to have bothered with. But God bothered. The grave was empty. The body was raised. Which means whatever heaven is, it is not the abandonment of the body. It is the body's vindication. And this changes how we grieve, how we hope, and how we live. C.S. Lewis, in the preface to The Great Divorce, warned against the easy belief that we can have heaven and earth both, that we can keep our cake and eat it, that the road out of the far country costs us nothing. He knew the popular picture was too small and too cheap. The real hope is larger and stranger and far more physical than the watercolor version we hang in funeral parlors. So why does it matter that most people, including most Christians, picture it wrong. Because the picture you hold of the end shapes the whole of how you live the middle. If heaven is escape, then this world is a waiting room, and your body is a rented suit, and the trees and the work and the marriage and the aching beauty of an October afternoon are all just temporary scaffolding to be torn down. But if heaven is the redemption of all of it, if the new earth is this earth healed, then nothing good is finally wasted. The cup of cold water counts. The garden you planted matters. The body you have learned to forgive will be raised. I have stood at too many gravesides and watched people comfort each other with a hope smaller than the one they were promised. She is an angel now. He is looking down on us. At peace, free of that broken body at last. And I have wanted to say, gently, that the Christian hope is better than that, and harder, and more solid. Not a soul set loose in the sky. A body in the ground that God has not finished with. A seed, Paul calls it, planted in dishonor, raised in glory. We have a country we have not seen. And we have been handing each other postcards of the wrong place. The work of this study is to put the right country back in front of us, in all its weight, and to let it do to us what the true hope always does. It does not make us less interested in this world. It makes us, finally, able to love it without clinging to it, and to face its loss without despair. That is where we are going. We have been picturing it wrong. Let us start seeing.

scriptureStudy.note: John sees a new heaven and a new earth, and the holy city coming down out of heaven from God. The direction is downward and earthward. The hope is not that we go up to God but that God comes down to dwell with us on a renewed creation.

The dwelling of God is with man, and he will wipe away every tear, and death shall be no more. The promise is not escape from the world but the end of what ruins it, death and mourning and pain, with God himself making his home among his people.

God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good. The material world is not a prison or a mistake but God's good work, which is why the hope is its redemption rather than its abandonment.

The risen Jesus shows his hands and feet, says a spirit does not have flesh and bones as he does, and eats a piece of fish. He goes out of his way to prove he is not a ghost, anchoring the hope in a raised body and not a freed soul.

Christ has been raised, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. His resurrection is the first sheaf of the harvest, the preview and guarantee of the bodily resurrection promised to all who are his.

The creation itself will be set free from its bondage to decay and brought into the freedom of the glory of the children of God. The earth is not slated for the dumpster but for liberation, waiting to be healed along with us.

Jesus says he goes to prepare a place and will come again and take us to himself. Even here the movement ends with his coming back, not with our permanent flight away, the Lord returning to be with his people.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the long quarrel between Athens and Jerusalem, because the wrong picture of heaven did not fall out of the sky, it was imported, and seeing the source helps the church repent of it. The Greek philosophical tradition, above all in its Platonic form, taught that the material body is a prison and the immortal soul a trapped spark whose salvation is to escape the flesh and return to the realm of pure spirit. The Hebrew Scriptures assume the opposite, that the body is good, that God made matter and called it very good, and that the human being is a unity of dust and breath, not a soul wearing a body like a coat. The early church inherited both streams and never fully sorted them, so that within a few centuries a Platonized otherworldliness had attached itself to Christian hope, and the resurrection of the body, which the creeds confess, quietly gave way in the popular imagination to the immortality of the soul, which the creeds do not. A serious group should weigh how deeply this borrowed picture still shapes Christian funerals, hymns, and comfort, and read the recovery of a more Hebraic, creational hope in writers like N.T. Wright against the lingering Platonism in much of what passes for heaven in the culture. The discipline is to let Scripture, and not Plato, set the shape of the hope, and to notice how much of what we assumed was Christian was Greek all along.

sessions.title: The Resurrection of the Body
sessions.aim: To recover the bodily resurrection and the redemption of creation as the actual Christian hope, what N.T. Wright calls life after life-after-death, and to see that this is the opposite of escapism.
sessions.summary: If you want to know what God plans for the world, look at what he did with Jesus on the third day. The resurrection is not a one-off exception to the rule that dead things stay dead. It is the first day of new creation breaking into the middle of the old, the firstfruits that guarantee the harvest. The first question is what the resurrection of Jesus reveals about our future and the world's. N.T. Wright names the place we have collapsed everything into. The popular hope is life after death, the soul with God. The Bible is far more interested in life after life-after-death, the resurrection of the body on a renewed earth, the room beyond the corridor. Bell takes the strong form of the doubt, that a physical resurrection is harder to believe than a surviving soul and that the church should quietly drop it. He refuses, because Paul refuses. If Christ has not been raised, Paul says, your faith is worthless, with no fallback to soul-survival. The body raised is a seed grown into a plant, continuity and transformation at once, recognizable and transfigured, like Jesus who could be touched and yet was no longer bound. Romans 8 says creation itself groans for liberation, not destruction. Then the turn. This is not escapism but its opposite. The man who believes his body will be raised cannot despise his body now, and the people who believe the earth will be healed cannot treat it as a dumpster. Your labor, Paul says, is not in vain. We were made for this world, healed.

keyScripture.why: Paul describes the resurrection body as a seed sown perishable and raised imperishable, sown in weakness and raised in power, naming the hope as a transformed physical body in continuity with this one, not a disembodied soul.

discussion.q: N.T. Wright distinguishes life after death, the soul with God, from life after life-after-death, the resurrection of the body on a new earth. Which of those have you spent your life hoping for, and which did you not know was promised?
discussion.behind: Open by naming the gap. Most people have only ever been offered the first and assume it is the whole. The aim is to surface that the destination is not the soul in heaven but the resurrection, and to let the room feel the corridor-versus-room distinction land.

discussion.q: Paul says if Christ has not been raised your faith is worthless, and offers no fallback to a surviving soul. Why does he stake everything on a physical resurrection rather than settling for the soul going to God?
discussion.behind: Press on why the bodily claim is non-negotiable. A soul-only hope needs no empty tomb. Help the room see that Paul will not trade resurrection for immortality, that the faith is resurrection or nothing, which is a far more concrete and falsifiable claim than vague survival.

discussion.q: Romans 8 says creation groans and waits to be set free from decay, not to be destroyed. How does it change your view of this physical world to learn it is slated for healing rather than the scrap heap?
discussion.behind: Move from the body to the cosmos. Many assume the earth gets burned and abandoned. The aim is to feel the scope of redemption, that the trees and oceans and the whole groaning order are waiting for liberation, which reframes how we treat creation now.

discussion.q: Lewis pictured heaven as more solid than earth, the grass so real it cut ghostly feet. We usually imagine the next life as vaporous and this one as concrete. Why might it be the reverse?
discussion.behind: Land the Lewis image. We instinctively think the spiritual is thin and the physical is dense. Help the room consider that the world to come is the realer, denser world and we are the ones who must be made substantial, which dignifies the body rather than dissolving it.

discussion.q: Bell confesses he spent years preaching a gospel of evacuation, getting souls to a safe place when they die. Where has your own faith shrunk the gospel to fit a funeral, leaving out the body and the earth?
discussion.behind: Close with self-implication. The aim is honest recognition that we have made the gospel too small, an exit strategy rather than the renewal of all things. Go first. The point is to feel the largeness of what Christ accomplished, not to add guilt.

objections.objection: A surviving soul I can almost believe. But bodies climbing out of graves, after they have decayed to nothing, is primitive and frankly embarrassing. The church should quietly drop the resurrection and keep the immortal soul.
objections.response: Bell refuses, and not because the objection is weak but because Paul already refused it, harder. In First Corinthians 15 Paul says that if Christ has not been raised, bodily, your faith is worthless and you are still in your sins, and he offers no consolation prize of a surviving soul. The faith is resurrection or it is nothing. As for the embarrassment, notice what Paul actually claims. Not the reassembly of old molecules but a seed and the plant that comes from it, continuity and transformation at once, the same you raised imperishable and powerful, no longer bound by the limits that killed you. The risen Jesus is the pattern, recognizable and touchable and able to eat, yet no longer held by locked doors or death. That is not a corpse reanimated and it is not a ghost. It is a new and denser kind of physical, and it is the whole hope. Trade it for an immortal soul and you have kept Plato and lost Christ.

objections.objection: If the world is going to be made new anyway, why bother caring for this one? Why fight for justice, plant gardens, or steward creation when it is all getting replaced?
objections.response: Because it is not getting replaced, it is getting redeemed, and the difference is everything. Romans 8 says creation will be set free from its bondage to decay, the same creation, liberated, not a different one swapped in. And Paul ends the great resurrection chapter not with leave it all behind but with this, that because the dead are raised, your labor in the Lord is not in vain. He does not promise that everything you build lasts in its present form. He promises that the Lord who raises the dead wastes nothing, that the cup of water and the just law and the planted orchard are somehow taken up, purified, and carried into the world that is coming. The hope of resurrection does not pull you out of the world. It plants you in it, with your sleeves rolled up, precisely because you know nothing done in love here is finally lost.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If you knew, all the way down, that your own body would be raised and this whole groaning earth healed rather than thrown away, what would you stop treating as disposable, and what would you start to love that you have been afraid to love because it dies?
sessions.practice: This week, choose one piece of the physical world you have treated as merely temporary, your own body, a patch of ground, a craft you make with your hands, a relationship that will end in a grave. Tend it deliberately, as if it mattered eternally, because in Christ it does. Care for the body. Plant the thing. Mend the bond. Then write down whether doing it as resurrection-work rather than waiting-room-work changed how it felt.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord of the empty tomb, you did not free your Son from his body, you raised it, and in raising it you showed us what you mean to do with us and with the whole groaning creation. Forgive us for hoping too small, for a gospel of evacuation that left out the body and the earth you died to redeem. Teach us that our labor in you is not in vain, that nothing done in love is wasted, that the world is not a waiting room but a field you are bringing to harvest. Make us people of the resurrection, with our hands in the dirt and our eyes on the morning, until the seed sown perishable is raised imperishable. Amen.
reflection: Have I hoped for life after death, the soul with God, and never reached for the fuller hope of life after life-after-death, the body raised on a healed earth?
Where has my gospel been an evacuation plan for souls rather than the renewal of all things that Scripture actually promises?
If my labor in the Lord is not in vain, what work of love am I tempted to think is wasted that God intends to take up and carry into the world to come?
sessions.teaching: If you want to know what God plans to do with the world, look at what he did with Jesus on the third day. The resurrection is not an isolated miracle, a one-time exception to the rule that dead things stay dead. It is the first day of the new creation breaking into the middle of the old. It is the preview. It is, Paul says, the firstfruits, the first sheaf of a harvest that guarantees the rest of the field is coming. N.T. Wright has a phrase for the place we have collapsed everything into. He calls the popular Christian hope life after death, and then says the Bible is far more interested in what he names life after life-after-death. There is a stage where the dead in Christ are with the Lord, conscious, at rest, waiting. That is real, and we will get to it. But it is not the end. It is the intermediate thing, the corridor, not the room. The end is resurrection. The end is new bodies on a new earth. To stop at life after death, the soul in God's presence, and call that the destination is to mistake the hallway for the home. Hear what Paul says in Romans 8, because it is one of the most ignored passages in the modern church and one of the most staggering. The creation itself, he says, was subjected to futility, and groans, and waits. It is not waiting to be discarded. It is waiting to be set free from its bondage to decay and brought into the freedom of the glory of the children of God. The trees are waiting. The oceans are waiting. The whole groaning, decaying, beautiful, broken physical order is waiting, not for the wrecking ball, but for redemption. God is not going to throw away the painting. He is going to restore it. This is why the bodily resurrection matters so much and why the early church died rather than deny it. A soul-only heaven needs no empty tomb. But the gospel stands or falls on a physical claim, that a dead man was buried and three days later was not in the grave, and was seen, and touched, and ate. Paul stakes everything on it in First Corinthians 15. If Christ has not been raised, he says, your faith is worthless and you are still in your sins and the dead are simply gone. He does not offer a fallback to soul-survival. No resurrection, no hope, full stop. The Christian faith is not the immortality of the soul with some Jesus added. It is resurrection or it is nothing. And the resurrection body is not a ghost and not a resuscitated corpse. Paul reaches for the image of a seed and the plant that comes from it. What is sown is perishable, what is raised is imperishable. There is continuity, it is really you, the same self, the same scarred and beloved you, and there is transformation, you are raised incorruptible, beyond death's reach. Jesus after the resurrection is the pattern. Recognizable, touchable, able to eat, bearing the wounds, and yet different, no longer bound by the old limits. That is the body promised to you. Not less physical than the one you have. More. Lewis gestured at this in The Great Divorce, where the newly arrived souls find the grass of heaven so real and so solid that it cuts their ghostly feet, and they are the thin ones, the unreal ones, until they grow more solid by drawing nearer to the source. He had the direction right. We tend to think of the next life as vaporous and this one as concrete. Lewis insisted it is the other way around. The world to come is the denser world, the realer one, and we are the ghosts who must be made substantial enough to bear it. So what does the new earth look like. The Bible is restrained but not silent. A city and a garden together, the cultivated and the wild reconciled. A river and a tree of life. No more sea, which to the ancient Hebrew meant no more chaos, no more of the deep dark that swallows ships and sailors. No more death, no more mourning, no more crying, no more pain, because the former things have passed away. And at the center, no temple, because the whole place is filled with the presence that the temple only ever pointed to. God dwelling with his people, on a renewed earth, in resurrected bodies, forever. I have to implicate myself here, because I spent years preaching a gospel that was really just about getting people's souls to a safe place when they died, a gospel of evacuation. Get saved so you go to the good place instead of the bad place when your body gives out. And that gospel is too small. It leaves out the body. It leaves out the earth. It leaves out the cosmic scope of what Christ accomplished, which Paul says is the reconciliation of all things, things in heaven and things on earth. I shrank the gospel to fit a funeral, and the real thing is the size of the universe. This is not escapism. This is the opposite of escapism. The man who believes his body will be raised cannot despise his body now. The people who believe the earth will be healed cannot treat the earth as a dumpster. The hope of resurrection does not pull us out of the world. It plants us in it, with our sleeves rolled up, because we know that what we do here in love is not swept away but somehow taken up, purified, and carried into the world that is coming. Your labor, Paul says at the end of the resurrection chapter, is not in vain. Not because everything you build lasts, but because the Lord who raises the dead wastes nothing. We were not made to escape this world. We were made for this world, healed. That is the country we have not seen, and it has dirt under its fingernails.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the doctrine the creeds confess and the church half forgot, the resurrection of the body and the life of the world to come, because the Apostles' Creed does not say I believe in the immortality of the soul, it says I believe in the resurrection of the body, and the difference is the whole argument of this session. Trace how the early church held a robustly physical hope, rooted in an empty tomb and a Lord who ate fish, against the pressure of a surrounding culture that found a surviving soul respectable and a rising body absurd. Set this beside the modern situation, in which the creed is still recited weekly in millions of churches while the people reciting it often mean by it nothing more than that grandma's soul is in a better place, so that the words confess resurrection while the heart believes Plato. A serious group should weigh the difference between immortality, something the Greeks thought the soul possessed by nature, and resurrection, something only God can do and only by sheer gift, raising the dead. Read N.T. Wright on the new creation alongside the older confessions, and ask what it would mean for a congregation to actually believe the line it sings at every funeral, that the bodies in the ground are seeds, and the God who emptied one tomb intends to empty them all. The discipline is to let the creed mean what it says.

memoryVerse.text: So is it with the resurrection of the dead. What is sown is perishable, what is raised is imperishable. It is sown in dishonor, it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness, it is raised in power.

sessions.title: Hell, Honestly
sessions.aim: To face the hardest doctrine without flinching and without gloating, laying out the historic view of eternal conscious punishment, the conditionalist view, and the reach of universalism each at full strength, so the room decides before God and not before a caricature.
sessions.summary: This is the session Bell would skip if he could, and that is exactly why he cannot. Hell is the hardest doctrine in the faith, and as an atheist it was the single thing he held hardest against God, the proof, as he saw it then, that the God of the Bible was a moral monster. The first question is the objection itself at full weight. How can a good God consign a finite creature to infinite conscious torment forever for the sins of a few decades. He will not pretend that is small. Then he lays three historic positions side by side, each at its strongest. The traditional view, eternal conscious punishment, held by Augustine, the Reformers, J.I. Packer, and Robert Peterson, grounded in the words of Jesus himself, who spoke of hell more than anyone, honoring the dreadful dignity of a creature who can say no to God forever, the door locked from the inside as Lewis pictured it in The Great Divorce. The conditionalist or annihilationist view, held tentatively by John Stott and argued by Edward Fudge in The Fire That Consumes, that immortality is a gift not an automatic possession, that Scripture's most common language is destruction and perishing, and that the lost finally cease to be. And universalism, the hope that all are saved, taken at its strongest in the love of God and the scope of the cross, then judged to overreach because it must either empty the warnings of Jesus or deny the creature the freedom to refuse love, which dissolves the love it wants to exalt. Bell holds the first two in tension and trembles. He refuses to gloat and refuses to flinch. What changed for him was not solving it but meeting the One who warned of the cliff and then went over it himself, into the dark, so that we would not have to. The Judge has the scars.

keyScripture.why: Jesus speaks of eternal punishment and eternal life in the same breath, the verse the traditional view reads as everlasting conscious punishment and the conditionalist reads as a destruction whose effect is eternal, the contested text both serious views must reckon with honestly.

discussion.q: Bell, a former atheist, says hell was the single thing he held hardest against God. What is your own honest reaction to the doctrine, and have you ever been allowed to say it out loud in church?
discussion.behind: Open by giving permission for the real objection. Many carry a buried horror about hell they have never been allowed to voice in a faith setting. The aim is honesty, not resolution. Let the room name the difficulty fully before any view is examined, and go first if needed.

discussion.q: State the objection at full weight. How can a good God consign a finite creature to infinite conscious torment forever for the sins of a few decades? Where does that disproportion land hardest on you?
discussion.behind: Do not rush to defend God here. The discipline of this session is to feel the force of the hardest objection first. The aim is to honor the question Bell honored, the disproportion between a finite life and an infinite penalty, so that whatever answer comes is not cheap.

discussion.q: Lay the three views out in your own words, the traditional eternal conscious punishment, the conditionalist view that the lost finally cease to be, and universalism. Which did you assume was the only Christian option, and which surprised you?
discussion.behind: Get the room to articulate all three fairly. Most have only heard the first and assume the others are heresy or wishful thinking. The aim is to see that two of these are held within orthodoxy by serious believers, which changes the tone from defending one to weighing several with humility.

discussion.q: Bell judges that universalism overreaches because it must either empty the warnings of Jesus or deny the creature the freedom to refuse love. Do you find that fair, and what is genuinely beautiful in the universalist hope that we should not lose?
discussion.behind: Hold both edges. The universalist impulse, that we long for no one to be lost, is near the heart of God. The overreach is knowing more than is revealed and dissolving the freedom love requires. Help the room honor the longing while seeing why Bell will not let it resolve what Scripture leaves open.

discussion.q: Bell says the person who speaks of the damnation of others with anything but tears has understood nothing. Where have you seen hell used as a weapon, and where have you been tempted to gloat or to flinch?
discussion.behind: Close with self-implication on both failures. The aim is to convict the gloater and the avoider at once, and to locate both temptations in ourselves. Jesus reserved his hottest words for the religious who enjoyed consigning others to hell. Go first, and keep it tender.

objections.objection: A God who tortures people consciously, forever, with no end and no exit, for the sins of one short life, is a moral monster. No amount of theology makes infinite punishment for finite crime anything but evil.
objections.response: Bell takes this at full weight because he made it himself as an atheist, and he will not insult you by shrinking it. The disproportion is the real scandal, and if you do not feel it you are not paying attention. Then he lays out how serious Christians have answered, at full strength and without forcing you. The traditional view replies that sin against an infinite God carries a weight we cannot measure, that the objection assumes we can calculate the gravity of rejecting our Maker, and that God honors freedom so completely he will not drag into his presence those who spent a life refusing it, the door of hell locked from the inside. The conditionalist view replies differently, that the objection has force, that Scripture's commonest language for the lost is destruction and perishing rather than endless preservation, and that the finally unrepentant are judged and then cease to be, justice served without an everlasting torture chamber. Both are held within orthodoxy. Bell holds the first two in tension and trembles, and refuses to hand you a tidy resolution, because the doctrine does not permit one.

objections.objection: Surely a loving God could not actually lose anyone. The cross is wide enough for all, every knee will bow, God will be all in all. In the end love wins and everyone comes home.
objections.response: Bell takes universalism at its strongest first, because the impulse behind it, that we long for no one to be lost, is not a sin, it is close to the heart of a God who takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked. The scope of the cross and the verses about reconciling all things deserve their full weight. Then he names where he judges it to overreach, carefully. To reach its conclusion universalism must do one of two things. It must empty the warnings of Jesus of their force, the warnings he gave more often and more vividly than anyone, which is a strange thing to do to the most loving man who ever lived. Or it must deny the creature the dreadful freedom to refuse God forever, which dissolves the very love it wants to exalt, because love that cannot be refused is not love but coercion. The gift is offered to all. But a gift can be refused, and Scripture and Jesus both seem to take with deadly seriousness that some do refuse it. Universalism tends to know more than has been revealed, resolving what Scripture leaves open.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Who is the person whose eternity you cannot bear to think about, and what does it do to you to hold their face in front of God in this hour rather than looking away?
sessions.practice: This week, do not argue about hell with anyone. Do something harder. Pick one person you love who is far from God, and instead of debating the doctrine, pray for them by name every day, with tears if they come, and let the weight of the question drive you to intercession rather than to either gloating or despair. Write down what it did to your own heart to carry a real person rather than an abstraction.
sessions.closingPrayer: Holy God, this is the doctrine we would rather not hold, and we will not pretend tonight that we have made it easy, because it is not easy and you have not asked us to lie. We confess the times we have used hell as a weapon and spoken of the lost without tears, and we confess the times we have flinched and edited out the warnings of your Son to make him more comfortable. Give us neither the cruelty of the gloater nor the cowardice of the one who looks away. We do not understand everything. We know this. The One who warned us of the dark walked into it himself, and came out with the scars, and can be trusted. Hold the ones we love, and hold us. Amen.
reflection: What is my honest objection to hell, and have I ever brought it to God directly rather than burying it or pretending it does not trouble me?
Of the three views laid out, which do I find myself leaning toward, and am I leaning there because of Scripture or because of what I wish were true?
Whom do I speak of, or think of, as deserving hell, and what would change if I could only think of the lost the way Jesus did, with tears?
sessions.teaching: This is the session I would skip if I could, and that is precisely why I cannot. Hell is the hardest doctrine in the Christian faith. It was, when I was an atheist, the single thing I held against the whole religion, the proof, as I saw it, that the God of the Bible was a moral monster, and I will not pretend now that I have made it comfortable. I have not. No one honest has. My task tonight is not to make hell easy. It is to refuse both flinching and gloating, to take the question as seriously as my younger self took it, and to lay the historic options in front of you at their full strength, so that you decide before God and not before a caricature. Start with the objection, the real one, not the cartoon. How can a good God consign a finite creature to infinite, conscious torment forever, with no end and no exit, for the sins of a few decades. The disproportion is the scandal. Seventy years of wrong, even terrible wrong, answered by an eternity of agony. I felt the full weight of that as an unbeliever, and I will not insult you by pretending it is a small thing. It is the largest thing. If you do not feel it, you are not paying attention. So we go slowly, and we do not gloat, because the doctrine of hell has been used by cruel people as a whip, and Jesus reserved his hottest words not for the sinners afraid of hell but for the religious who enjoyed consigning others to it. Now the views, each at full strength, none knocked down with a straw man. First, the historic and traditional view, eternal conscious punishment. This is the majority position across most of church history, held by Augustine, by the Reformers, and in our own time defended carefully by men like J.I. Packer and Robert Peterson. It holds that hell is real, conscious, and everlasting, the just and final separation of those who reject God from the God they rejected. Its strength is considerable, and you must feel it. The words of Jesus himself are its ground, more than anyone else in Scripture. He spoke of eternal fire, of the worm that does not die, of outer darkness, of a great fixed chasm. The traditional view takes those words at face value and refuses to soften what the Son of God did not soften. It argues that sin against an infinite God carries infinite weight, that the disproportion objection assumes we can measure the gravity of rejecting our Maker, and that we cannot. It insists that God honors human freedom all the way down, that he will not drag into his presence those who have spent a life refusing it, that the door of hell, as Lewis put it, is locked from the inside. C.S. Lewis gives this its most humane form in The Great Divorce, where the damned are not tortured against their will but cling, freely, to their misery, choosing the grey town over the mountains again and again. The strength of this view is that it honors the plain weight of Jesus' warnings and the terrible dignity of a creature able to say to God, finally and forever, no. Second, the conditionalist or annihilationist view. This is the minority report, but it is not new and not fringe, and serious evangelicals hold it. John Stott, one of the towering evangelical figures of the last century, confessed near the end of his life that he leaned toward it, tentatively and with trembling. Edward Fudge made the long biblical case in his book The Fire That Consumes. Conditionalism holds that immortality is not something the soul automatically possesses but a gift God gives to the redeemed, that the wages of sin is death, real death, and that the finally unrepentant are not kept alive forever in torment but are judged, and then perish, and cease to be. Its strength is also considerable, and you must feel it too. It takes seriously that Scripture's most common language for the lost is destruction, perishing, death, being consumed, the chaff burned up, not endless preservation. It points out that the immortality of the soul, the assumption that we must exist forever somewhere, is the very Platonic idea we questioned in session one. It argues that the eternal in eternal punishment can mean a punishment whose effect is eternal, a destruction that is final and unreversible, rather than an eternally ongoing experience of being punished. And it answers the disproportion objection with weight, that justice is served, fully, but that God does not maintain a never-ending torture chamber across the ages of ages. Do not dismiss it as wishful softness. Stott was no liberal, and the case is biblical, and it must be met biblically. Third, universalism, the hope that all will finally be saved. Here I will be honest about where I think it overreaches, and I will still take it at its strongest first. Its strength is the love of God and the scope of the cross, the verses that speak of God reconciling all things, of every knee bowing, of God being all in all, of his will that none should perish. The universalist asks how a love that strong, a cross that wide, could finally lose anyone, and whether hell, if it exists, might be remedial rather than final, a fire that purifies until even the most stubborn at last turn home. It is a beautiful hope, and the impulse behind it, that we long for no one to be lost, is not a sin. It is close to the heart of God, who takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked. But here is where I judge it to overreach, and I say judge carefully. Universalism, to arrive at its conclusion, must finally do one of two things. It must either empty the warnings of Jesus of their force, the warnings he gave more often and more vividly than anyone, which is a strange thing to do to the most loving man who ever lived, or it must deny the creature the dreadful freedom to refuse God forever, which dissolves the very love it wants to exalt, because love that cannot be refused is not love but coercion. The cross is wide enough for all. But a gift can be refused, and Scripture and Jesus both seem to take with deadly seriousness that some do refuse it, finally. Universalism, for all its beauty, tends to know more than has been revealed. It resolves what Scripture leaves unresolved. And the unresolved warning is there for a reason, because a hell you can presume your way out of is a hell that has stopped doing the one thing Jesus used it to do, which is to make you take your life, and your choices, and your neighbor, with eternal seriousness. So where does that leave us. It leaves us, I think, between the first view and the second, both held within orthodoxy, both wrestling honestly with the same texts, both refusing the easy exit of presuming everyone home regardless. I will not tell you which of the first two to hold. I hold them in tension and tremble. What I will tell you is this. Do not gloat about hell. Ever. The person who speaks of the damnation of others with anything but tears has understood nothing. And do not flinch from it either, because Jesus did not, and a Christianity that has edited out the warnings of Christ to make him more palatable has kept the comfort and thrown away the Lord. I came to faith as a man who hated this doctrine. I will tell you what changed. Not that I solved it. I did not. What changed is that I met the One who spoke of it, and saw that he spoke of it the way a man speaks of a cliff to a child he loves, and then walked toward the cliff himself and went over it, into the dark, so that I would not have to. Whatever hell is, the God who warns of it is the God who descended into it. That does not answer every question. It answers the only one that finally matters, which is whether the Judge can be trusted. He can. He has the scars.

scriptureStudy.note: These will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life. The traditional view reads the parallel as everlasting conscious punishment, the conditionalist reads eternal as describing a destruction whose result is final and unending. The contested verse both must face.

Where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched. Jesus draws on Isaiah's image of judgment. The traditional view hears unending conscious torment, the conditionalist hears the unquenchable fire that fully consumes, the image both sides read differently.

Fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell. The word destroy is the conditionalist's central text, while the traditional view reads destruction as ruin rather than annihilation. A verse that cuts toward the conditionalist case and must be weighed.

Death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire, the second death. The phrase the second death names the lost end as a death, which the conditionalist reads as a real ceasing, while the traditional view reads the lake of fire as conscious and unending.

They will suffer the punishment of eternal destruction, away from the presence of the Lord. The pairing of eternal with destruction is exactly the language both views contest, an eternal destroying or a destruction that is eternal in its effect.

God desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. The universalist's strong ground, the genuine will of God that none be lost, which must be held alongside the warnings rather than used to cancel them.

How often would I have gathered your children, and you were not willing. Jesus weeps over the city that refuses him, naming both the depth of his longing and the dreadful reality of a refusal he will not override, the freedom love requires.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the actual history of the doctrine, because the debate this session lays out is older and more orthodox on multiple sides than most congregations are told. The traditional view of eternal conscious punishment became the dominant position in the West, shaped powerfully by Augustine, carried by the medieval church, and affirmed by the Reformers, and it has able modern defenders in writers such as J.I. Packer and Robert Peterson who ground it chiefly in the words of Jesus. But conditionalism is not a modern invention either, it has roots in the early centuries and surfaces again and again, and in the twentieth century it gained a serious hearing when John Stott, a pillar of evangelicalism, confessed he leaned toward it, and when Edward Fudge laid out the sustained biblical case in The Fire That Consumes. Universalism, in its Christian form, traces back to figures like Origen and has had a long, contested afterlife, condemned at points yet never fully absent, recurring wherever the love of God is pressed against the fate of the lost. A serious group should read each position in its strongest primary advocates rather than in its opponents' summaries, weigh the key contested texts directly, and resist the twin temptations of treating a contested question as settled and treating a serious question as merely a matter of taste. The discipline is to hold strong convictions humbly, to grant that faithful believers have read the same Scriptures and landed in different places, and to let the weight of the matter drive the room to its knees rather than to its corners.

memoryVerse.text: The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance.

sessions.title: The Dead in Christ
sessions.aim: To sit honestly with what happens when we die, the intermediate state and the communion of saints, and to hold grief and hope together at the graveside without letting go of either.
sessions.summary: What happens the moment after you die, not at the end of all things but that very moment when the breath goes out. The Bible says less than we want and more than we notice, and the gap is where bad theology and needless grief grow. The first question is what we are actually promised. Bell clears away what we are not promised, that we become angels, that the dead are simply gone, that the moment of death is the final state. Then the promise. To be absent from the body is to be present with the Lord. The thief is told, today you will be with me in paradise. The dead in Christ are immediately and consciously with him, at rest, home, safe. This is the intermediate state, and the word matters, in between, because they are with the Lord and that is unspeakably good and it is still not the end. They are not yet raised. They wait, conscious and content but expectant, for the resurrection morning. The martyrs under the altar are home and still crying how long. This is why the church confesses the communion of saints, one church in two rooms, and Eugene Peterson insisted it is not poetry but the structure of the thing. Then grief, because it is abstract until it is your father in the box. Bell, raised without a father, will not pretend the doctrine removes the grief. Paul does not say do not grieve. He says do not grieve as those with no hope. The hope does not cancel the grief, it changes its color. We weep at a train platform, not a tomb. The one we love has gone ahead, not gone out. Lewis in A Grief Observed found not the end of pain but a solid confidence that she was only ahead. Hold the two together. Grief and hope. He does not know everything about the country beyond the grave. He knows who is there. That has turned out to be enough.

keyScripture.why: Paul tells the grieving not to grieve as those who have no hope, because Jesus died and rose and God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep, naming a grief that is real and a hope that is sure, held together rather than canceling each other.

discussion.q: What have you believed happens the moment after a Christian dies, and where did that belief come from, Scripture, a hymn, a funeral, or a guess you never examined?
discussion.behind: Open by surfacing the inherited picture. Many hold vague or contradictory ideas, soul sleep, instant heaven, becoming an angel, with no idea which is biblical. The aim is to expose the assumptions gently before laying out what Scripture actually promises about the intermediate state.

discussion.q: Paul says to be absent from the body is to be present with the Lord, and Jesus tells the thief, today you will be with me in paradise. What comfort, and what mystery, is in that word today?
discussion.behind: Land the immediacy. The dead in Christ are not unconscious and not waiting in a void, they are with the Lord at once. Help the room feel the comfort of today while honoring how little detail we are given, so the comfort does not curdle into speculation.

discussion.q: Bell calls this the intermediate state, the corridor and not the room, because even the faithful dead are not yet raised and still wait for the resurrection. Why does it matter that being with the Lord is not yet the end?
discussion.behind: Press on the in-between. Connect this session to sessions one and two, that the soul with Christ is real but the destination is bodily resurrection on the new earth. The aim is to keep the full hope in view, that even the dead are leaning forward toward the morning.

discussion.q: The church confesses the communion of saints, one church in two rooms. How does it change your sense of the people you have buried to think of them as more deeply joined to Christ now, not severed from the body but ahead of you in it?
discussion.behind: Land the communion of saints as Peterson framed it, structure and not sentiment. The aim is to ease the felt distance of the grave, to help the room sense the dead in Christ as near in the deep order of things, separated by a thin wall and a short time.

discussion.q: Paul does not say do not grieve, he says do not grieve as those with no hope. Where have you felt pressure to skip the grief and perform the hope, and what would it look like to hold both honestly?
discussion.behind: Close with self-implication and tenderness. Many Christians feel guilty for grieving, as though faith should erase the pain. The aim is to give permission to weep fully while weeping toward a morning. Go first, and be gentle, because there will be fresh grief in the room.

objections.objection: If my mother is already with the Lord in heaven, why does the Bible also talk about a future resurrection? Either she is already there and the resurrection is pointless, or she is not and you have been lying to grieving people.
objections.response: Neither, and the answer is the word intermediate. Your mother, if she is in Christ, is with the Lord now, consciously, at rest, and that is true and unspeakably good. To be absent from the body is to be present with the Lord. But that is not yet the end, it is the corridor and not the room. She is not yet raised, her body is still in the ground, and she waits, content but expectant, for the resurrection morning when body and soul are rejoined and she stands whole on the new earth. The resurrection is not pointless, it is the destination the intermediate state is waiting for. Even the martyrs in Revelation, pictured at rest under the altar, still cry out how long. Home and still waiting, both at once. You have not been lied to. You have been told only half, and the other half is better, because it ends not with a soul in the sky but with your mother raised.

objections.objection: If I really believed my loved ones were in a better place and I would see them again, I would not grieve like this. My grief proves my faith is weak, or proves I do not actually believe any of it.
objections.response: Hold this one with great care, because it is shame laid on top of sorrow, and Paul cuts it off at the root. He does not tell the grieving Thessalonians not to grieve. He tells them not to grieve as those who have no hope, which means Christian grief is real grief, full weight, honest tears, because death is real and the separation is a genuine wound. Hope does not cancel the grief, it changes its color. You weep, but you weep at a train platform and not a tomb, for someone gone ahead and not gone out. Lewis wrote A Grief Observed in raw anguish after his wife died and did not tidy it up, and his faith did not spare him the pain, it carried him through it to a solid confidence that she was only ahead. Your grief is not the failure of your faith. It is love with nowhere to put itself yet, and the gospel does not forbid it. It gives it a morning to face.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Who is the person you most long to see again, and what would it mean to believe tonight that they are not lost in the dark but with the Lord, ahead of you on a road you are both still traveling?
sessions.practice: This week, name your dead before God. Take one person you have lost in Christ, say their name out loud in prayer, and instead of pushing the grief away or pretending it is fine, let yourself feel it fully while you say the true thing over it. You are with the Lord. You are not lost. I will see you in the morning. Write down what it was like to grieve and hope in the same breath rather than choosing one.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord of the living and the dead, you hold the ones we have buried as surely as you hold us, and they are not lost, only ahead, with you, at rest, waiting as we wait for the morning when the graves are opened. We bring you our grief, the real and heavy weight of it, and we will not pretend it away, because you wept at the tomb of your friend before you raised him. Teach us to grieve as people with hope and not as people with none. Keep the ones we love until the resurrection, and keep us until we see them, and you, face to face. We do not know everything about that country. We know who is there. Let that be enough. Amen.
reflection: What have I assumed about the moment after death, and does it match the Bible's promise that the dead in Christ are immediately and consciously with the Lord, yet still awaiting the resurrection?
Have I felt that my grief was a failure of faith, and what changes if Paul permits real grief as long as it is grief toward hope and not despair?
Who have I buried in Christ, and what would it mean to live as though they are not severed from me but ahead of me, in the same church, separated by a thin wall and a short time?
sessions.teaching: What happens the moment after you die. Not at the end of all things, but that very moment, when the heart stops and the breath goes out. The Bible says less about this than we want and more than we usually notice, and the gap between the two is where a lot of bad theology and a lot of unnecessary grief have grown up. Start with what we are not promised, because clearing it away helps. We are not promised that we become angels. Angels are a different order of being, and your dead mother did not get her wings, because she was never going to be an angel, she was going to be something greater, a resurrected human being, which outranks the angels in the economy of God. We are not promised that the dead are simply gone, asleep in a nothingness until the end. And we are not promised that the moment of death is the final state. It is not. It is the doorway to the corridor, not the door to the room. Here is what we are promised. To be absent from the body is to be present with the Lord. Paul says it plainly, that to depart and be with Christ is far better, and he does not say better than living, he says far better, which is an astonishing thing to say about death unless he knew something. The thief on the cross is told, today you will be with me in paradise. Today. Not at the end of the age, but that very day. So the consistent witness is that those who die in Christ are, immediately and consciously, with him. At rest. At peace. Awake, not asleep in the sense of unconscious, but home, and safe, and aware of the One they loved and longed for. This is the intermediate state, and the old word for it matters, intermediate, in between. The dead in Christ are with the Lord, and that is unspeakably good, and it is still not the end. They are not yet raised. Their bodies are still in the ground. They wait, as we wait, conscious and content but expectant, for the resurrection morning when the bodies come up and the whole person, body and soul rejoined, stands on the new earth. Even the faithful dead are not finished. Even they are leaning forward, waiting for the trumpet. The book of Revelation pictures the martyrs under the altar, alive, at rest, and yet crying out, how long. Home, and still waiting. Both at once. This is why the church has always confessed the communion of saints, and why that phrase is one of the great underused comforts of the faith. The church is not divided by death into the living who matter and the dead who are gone. It is one church, in two rooms. The church militant, us, still fighting, still grieving, still walking by faith. And the church triumphant, them, at rest with the Lord, the great cloud of witnesses the writer of Hebrews says surrounds us. Eugene Peterson spent his life insisting that the communion of saints is not poetry but plumbing, the actual structure of the thing, that the people you have loved and buried are not severed from the body of Christ but more deeply joined to its Head than ever. You are not as far from them as the grave makes it feel. You are in the same church. You are separated by a thin wall and a short time. The older Christians knew this and lived inside it. They named their dead at the table, they kept their days, they told their stories to children who never met them, not to traffic with the dead but because the dead in Christ were still family, still members, still part of the body praying its way toward the same morning. We have largely lost that, and the loss has cost us. We treat the grave as a final wall and the departed as simply absent, and then we wonder why our grief feels so cut off, so much like staring into a blank. But the wall is thinner than it looks. The people you have buried in Christ are not on the far side of an abyss. They are in the next room of the same house, awake before the same Lord, waiting for the same trumpet that you are waiting for. And now I have to speak about grief, because all of this is abstract until it is your father in the box, your child in the small grave, your wife of forty years suddenly an empty side of the bed. I have buried people I loved. I was raised without a father, and I have felt the particular ache of grieving a presence I barely had, and I will not stand here and tell you that the doctrine of the intermediate state makes the grief go away. It does not. It is not supposed to. Paul does not tell the grieving Thessalonians not to grieve. Read it carefully. He tells them not to grieve as those who have no hope. The hope does not cancel the grief. It changes its color. The Christian at the graveside weeps, really weeps, with the full weight of loss, because death is real and the separation is real and the absence is a wound. But the Christian weeps as someone standing at a train platform, not a tomb. The one we love has gone ahead, not gone out. We are not waving at a vanishing. We are waiting for a reunion. Lewis, who wrote A Grief Observed in the raw aftermath of his wife's death and did not tidy up his anguish for the reader, came finally not to a removal of the pain but to a strange and solid confidence that she was not lost, only ahead, and that the God who held her held him too. So hold the two together, because the gospel always holds them together and never lets you drop one. Grief and hope. Tears that are honest and a hope that is sure. The faith does not ask you to pretend the death did not gut you. It asks you to grieve toward a morning. The dead in Christ are with Christ. They are safe. They are nearer to you, in the deep structure of things, than the silence of the phone suggests. And one day the same Lord who keeps them now will raise them, bodily, on the new earth, and the long separation will be revealed for what it always was, not an ending, but an absence between two presences, a held breath before the door opens. I do not know everything about the country beyond the grave. I know who is there. That has turned out to be enough.

scriptureStudy.note: We would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord. Paul names death for the believer as a homecoming, immediate presence with Christ, not an unconscious sleep and not a void.

Truly I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise. Jesus promises the dying thief presence with him that very day, the strongest word in the Gospels for the immediacy of the intermediate state.

My desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better. Paul calls death far better, not because the body is escaped but because it brings him at once into the presence of the Lord he loves, while still awaiting the resurrection.

The souls under the altar cry out how long, and are told to rest a little longer. The faithful dead are conscious and at rest and yet still waiting, home and expectant at once, which is exactly the shape of the intermediate state.

We are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses. The faithful dead are not severed from the church but joined to it, the communion of saints, near to us in the deep structure of the body of Christ.

Do not grieve as those who have no hope, for God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep. Paul permits real grief and forbids only hopeless grief, holding sorrow and certainty together rather than canceling one with the other.

I am the resurrection and the life, whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live. Jesus says this at the tomb of a friend, and weeps even as he speaks it, joining the surest hope to the most honest grief.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the phrase the creed has had us confess for centuries and most of us have never weighed, the communion of saints, because it carries more comfort than nearly any line in Christian teaching and is almost never preached. The phrase confesses that the church is not divided by death into the living who count and the dead who are gone, but is one body in Christ, joined across the grave, the church still struggling on earth and the church at rest with the Lord bound together in him. The older tradition spoke of this with a confidence the modern church has largely lost, and Eugene Peterson, among others, insisted in his pastoral writing that the communion of saints is not a sentimental flourish but the actual architecture of the thing, that the people we have loved and buried are more deeply joined to the Head of the body than ever. A serious group should weigh how the Protestant recovery rightly guarded against praying to the dead or trafficking with them, while sometimes overcorrecting into a practical silence that leaves the grieving feeling utterly cut off from those they have lost. Read the cloud of witnesses in Hebrews and the souls under the altar in Revelation against the modern experience of the grave as a final wall, and ask what it would mean for a congregation to live as though the dead in Christ were in the next room rather than in oblivion. The discipline is to recover the comfort without the superstition, to know the beloved dead as near in Christ, ahead of us on the same road, awaiting the same morning.

memoryVerse.text: We do not want you to be uninformed, brothers, about those who are asleep, that you may not grieve as others do who have no hope.

sessions.title: The Long Defeat and the Final Morning
sessions.aim: To bring the whole study home to the present, showing how the end shapes the middle, how the true hope produces courage rather than escapism or accommodation, and how we live the long defeat with our eyes on the morning that is coming.
sessions.summary: We have spent four sessions on the end. The question that decides whether it was worth the evenings is this. So what. What does the end do to the middle. There are two wrong answers, and the church has tried both. The first is escapism, the eschatology of the bunker, where the world is doomed and the faithful hunker down and let the rest rot, Christians who will not plant trees because the orchard is doomed. Session two already refuted it, because the earth is healed and not burned. The second wrong answer is its mirror, a Christianity so embarrassed by heaven and hell that it drops them and shrinks to a program for making this world slightly more pleasant, hope for the afternoon and none for the dead, nothing to say at the only graveside that matters, your own. Between the bunker and the chaplaincy stands the thing the New Testament teaches, and it is fierce. The hope of resurrection makes you dangerous to despair, because it tells you two things at once, that this world is worth fighting for since it will be redeemed and not discarded, and that you do not have to win for it to matter, since the outcome is in the hands of the One who raises the dead. You can fight a losing battle without despair because you know who wins the war. Tolkien called the Christian life the long defeat, the slow erosion, the cause that loses ground, and underneath it the final morning, what he called eucatastrophe, the good catastrophe, the sudden joyous turn when all seemed lost. The resurrection is the eucatastrophe of all history. Lewis reached for it at the end of Narnia, the morning when the holidays begin and every chapter is better than the one before. Bell, who has lived enough of the long defeat to be tempted by both wrong answers, finds the true hope rebuking both. We live with our hands in the dirt of this world and our eyes on the dawn of the next, planting orchards for grandchildren we may never meet, fighting the long defeat with the courage of people who have read the last page. It ends with a morning. The morning is always the end.

keyScripture.why: God wipes away every tear and declares behold, I am making all things new, naming the final morning toward which the long defeat runs, the hope that lets us labor now without despair because we have been told how the story ends.

discussion.q: Now that we have spent four sessions on the end, ask the blunt question. So what? What difference has it actually made, or not made, to how you are living the middle?
discussion.behind: Open by gathering the whole study and demanding it pay out in life. The aim is to move from doctrine to consequence, to surface whether the hope has changed anything yet. Let honest answers come, including the honest answer that it has not changed much, which is its own starting point.

discussion.q: Bell names two wrong answers, the bunker that flees a doomed world and the chaplaincy that drops the horizon and just makes the present nicer. Which of the two are you more tempted toward, and why?
discussion.behind: Get the room to locate themselves between the two errors. Most lean one way, either pious withdrawal or a faith embarrassed by heaven and hell. The aim is honest self-placement, so the true hope can rebuke the temptation each person actually has rather than an abstract one.

discussion.q: The true hope says this world is worth fighting for and you do not have to win for it to matter. How would your week change if you could labor hard at a losing battle without despair, because you knew who wins the war?
discussion.behind: Land the central freedom. Many work either anxiously, as if everything depends on their winning, or not at all, having given up. Help the room feel the courage that comes from a secured outcome, the freedom to fight the long defeat without it crushing them.

discussion.q: Tolkien called the Christian life the long defeat with a final morning underneath it, and the resurrection the eucatastrophe, the sudden joyous turn when all seemed lost. Where in your life are you in the long defeat right now, and what would it mean to believe a morning is coming?
discussion.behind: Let people name their actual long defeats, the failing body, the prodigal child, the cause that loses ground. The aim is to set real present loss against the promise of eucatastrophe, so the hope is not abstract but spoken over the specific dark each person is in.

discussion.q: Looking back over all five sessions, what is the one thing about the life to come you most want to carry out of this room, and how do you want it to change the way you live this week?
discussion.behind: Close the whole study with self-implication and commission. Do not resolve it neatly. Invite each person, the leader first, to name what they are carrying out and how it will land in the ordinary week. The point is to send the room into the long defeat with eyes on the morning.

objections.objection: All this talk about heaven just makes Christians useless on earth. Pie in the sky when you die. People so heavenly minded they are no earthly good, ignoring real suffering because they are waiting to be raptured out.
objections.response: Bell grants that this version exists and has done real damage, the eschatology of the bunker that will not plant trees because the orchard is doomed. But it gets the true hope exactly backwards. If the world were going to burn and only souls escape, the bunker would make sense. But session two showed the earth is going to be healed, not discarded, and a hope of healing does not produce people who abandon the patient, it produces people who fight for it. The believer who knows his body will be raised cannot despise his body now, and the people who know the earth will be made new cannot treat it as a dumpster. The most world-engaged people in history have often been those most sure of the world to come, because they could pour themselves out without fear of final loss. Heavenly mindedness rightly understood does not pull you off the earth. It plants you in it, freed from despair, able to labor at a losing battle because you know who wins the war.
