objections.objection: It is fine to say a glorious morning is coming, but I am living in the long defeat now. My body is failing, my child has walked away from God, the cause I gave my life to is losing. The promise of the end does not touch the pain of the middle.
objections.response: Bell will not pretend it removes the pain, because it does not, and he has lived enough of the long defeat to know better than to offer you that. Tolkien was right that history is mostly the long defeat, the slow erosion, the cause that loses ground, and the Christian is not promised that the good visibly wins in this age. What you are promised is what Tolkien called eucatastrophe, the good catastrophe, the sudden joyous turn when all seemed lost, of which the resurrection is the first and the guarantee. The end does not erase the middle, but it tells you the middle is not the last word, because the darkest Friday in history was not the last word either. So you do not have to win to be faithful. You plant the orchard you will not see fruit, you keep praying for the child, you fight the losing cause, not because you will see the victory here, but because the One who raises the dead has read the last page to you, and it ends with a morning.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If you truly believed that the long defeat you are living now ends not in the grave but in a morning, with every tear wiped away by a hand that has scars in it, what would you have the courage to do, or to keep doing, this week?
sessions.practice: This week, do one deliberate act of resurrection hope in the middle of your long defeat. Plant something you will not see mature. Begin a work you may not finish. Love someone whose return you cannot guarantee. Keep praying for the one who has walked away. Do it not because you expect to see the victory soon, but as a declaration that you have read the last page and you know how the story ends. Write down what it cost you and what it freed in you.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord of the morning, we have lived the long defeat, the slow erosion, the bodies that fail and the causes that lose and the children who wander, and we have been tempted to flee the world or to give up the horizon and call it wisdom. Forgive us both. You have not promised us the victory in this age. You have promised us the morning, the good catastrophe, the sudden joyous turn that your empty tomb already began. Make us people who plant orchards we will not see, who fight losing battles without despair, who love without guarantee, because we have read the last page and we know who waits at the gate. We have not seen that country. Give us the courage to live now in the light of then. Until the morning. Amen.
reflection: So what? After five sessions on the life to come, what has actually changed, or needs to change, in how I am living the middle?
Am I more tempted to flee this world as doomed or to shrink my faith to a program for making the present nicer, and how does the true hope rebuke my particular temptation?
Where am I in the long defeat right now, and what would it mean to labor there with the courage of someone who has read the last page and knows a morning is coming?
sessions.teaching: We have spent four sessions on the end, the wrong picture and the right one, the resurrection and the new earth, hell at its hardest, the dead in Christ and the communion of saints. The question that decides whether any of it was worth your evenings is this. So what. What does the end do to the middle. How does the country we have not seen change the way we live in the country we are stuck in. There are two wrong answers, and the church has tried both. The first wrong answer is escapism. If this world is going to burn and only souls go up, then nothing here matters much, and the faithful response is to hunker down, wait it out, keep your own soul clean and a few others, and let the rest of the rotting world rot. This is the eschatology of the bunker. It has produced Christians who will not plant trees because the orchard is doomed, who treat justice and beauty and the groaning of the poor as distractions from the only thing that counts, getting out. We saw in session two why it is false. The earth is not going to burn to nothing. It is going to be healed. And a hope of healing does not produce people who abandon the patient. The second wrong answer is its mirror, the loss of the end altogether, a Christianity so embarrassed by heaven and hell that it quietly drops them and becomes a program for making this present world slightly more pleasant, a chaplaincy to the status quo with no horizon beyond the next election. This one does not flee the world. It shrinks to fit it. It has hope for the afternoon and none for the dead, and so it has, finally, nothing to say at the only graveside that matters, your own. Between the bunker and the chaplaincy stands the thing the New Testament actually teaches, and it is fierce. The hope of the resurrection and the new earth does not make you less engaged with this world. It makes you dangerous to despair. It is the only hope that produces courage instead of either escape or accommodation, because it tells you two things at once that nothing else holds together. It tells you that this world is worth fighting for, because it is going to be redeemed, not discarded, so the cup of water and the just law and the planted garden and the loved enemy all count, all get taken up into the world that is coming, none of it wasted. And it tells you that you do not have to win for it to matter, because the outcome is not finally in your hands, it is in the hands of the One who raises the dead, so you are freed from the crushing weight of having to secure the victory yourself. You can fight a losing battle without despair, because you know who wins the war. Tolkien had a phrase for this that has carried me through years I could not see the end of. He called the Christian life the long defeat. He wrote that history is a long defeat, containing only samples and glimpses of final victory. That sounds bleak until you understand it. The follower of Christ is not promised that the good wins in this age. We are promised, mostly, the long defeat, the slow erosion, the cause that loses ground, the body that fails, the world that does not get visibly better on our watch. And we are promised, underneath and beyond the long defeat, the final morning. Tolkien coined another word for it, eucatastrophe, the good catastrophe, the sudden joyous turn when all seemed lost, the dawn that breaks precisely when the night was darkest and the battle plainly lost. The resurrection is the eucatastrophe of all history, the morning that came after the Friday when everything had ended. And it is the promise that our long defeats are not the last word, because his was not. Lewis said it in his own register at the end of the Narnia books, the line about the morning when the dream is over and the term holidays have begun, when chapter one of the great story which no one on earth has read begins, the story which goes on forever, in which every chapter is better than the one before. He was reaching, the way you reach for something too large to hold, toward the truth that what waits for us is not less than this life but immeasurably more, and that our deepest experiences here, the ones that broke our hearts with longing, were postcards from a country we are going home to. And I have to put myself inside this last, because I am the man who has lived enough of the long defeat to be tempted by both wrong answers. I have wanted to flee, to stop caring about a world that breaks my heart, to pull my five sons close and let the rest of it go dark. And I have wanted, in my tired and faithless hours, to give up the horizon altogether and just make things a little nicer and call it gospel. The true hope rebukes both my temptations. It will not let me flee, because the world is going to be healed and I am called to plant the first seeds of it now. And it will not let me shrink, because there is a morning coming that is larger than every defeat I will suffer between now and the grave. So how do we live now in light of then. We live with our hands in the dirt of this world and our eyes on the dawn of the next, doing the next right thing, loving the people God has given us, building things we will not see finished, planting orchards for grandchildren we may never meet, refusing both the bunker and the chaplaincy, fighting the long defeat with the courage of people who have read the last page and know how the story ends. It ends with a morning. It ends with the dead raised and the earth healed and every tear wiped away by a hand with scars in it. We have not seen that country. But we know the road runs toward it, and we know who is waiting at the gate. So we get up, and we love, and we labor, and we do not lose heart, because the night, however long, is not the end. The morning is the end. The morning is always the end.

scriptureStudy.note: He will wipe away every tear, and death shall be no more, and he says behold, I am making all things new. The final morning of all history, the end the whole long defeat runs toward, every former thing undone by the One who renews all things.

Therefore be steadfast, immovable, knowing that in the Lord your labor is not in vain. Paul draws the practical edge of resurrection hope, the steadiness to keep laboring because nothing done in the Lord is finally wasted.

The sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed. Paul weighs the long defeat against the morning and finds the present pain real but outweighed, not denied but set in scale.

They died in faith, not having received the things promised, but having seen them from afar, desiring a better country. The faithful lived and died in the long defeat, courageous because they hoped for a country they had not yet seen.

Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day, for this light momentary affliction is preparing an eternal weight of glory. The body fails in the long defeat while the hope grows, the seen passing and the unseen eternal.

Waiting for the hope we long for, the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ. The Christian posture is active waiting, eyes on the appearing, a hope that orients the whole of the present life.

He who testifies to these things says, surely I am coming soon. Amen. Come, Lord Jesus. The Bible ends with a longing for the morning, the church answering the promise of his coming with a prayer for it, which is how we live now in light of then.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the literary witnesses who taught a generation to feel the shape of Christian hope, because Tolkien and Lewis did something theologians often could not, they made the long defeat and the final morning imaginable. Tolkien, in his essay on fairy stories, coined the word eucatastrophe for the sudden joyous turn at the darkest moment of a tale, the unexpected deliverance that does not deny the sorrow but pierces it with a joy as sharp as grief, and he argued that the Resurrection is the eucatastrophe of the whole human story, the place where the deepest longing of every good tale turns out to be true. His phrase the long defeat, spoken in his larger work, names the Christian's experience of history as a fighting retreat that nevertheless guards glimpses of the victory to come. Lewis reached for the same truth at the close of the Narnia stories, the image of death as the end of the holidays of the old world and the first morning of a great story which goes on forever, every chapter better than the one before, and across his work the theme of joy as a longing for a country we have not seen but were made for. A serious group should weigh how imagination and story carry the hope into places argument cannot reach, and ask what it means that our deepest experiences of beauty and longing here may be, as Lewis put it, the scent of a flower we have not found and the echo of a tune we have not heard. The discipline is to let the witnesses train the affections, so that the hope is not only believed but desired, and so that the long defeat is endured by people who have learned to ache, rightly, for the morning.

memoryVerse.text: And he who was seated on the throne said, Behold, I am making all things new. Also he said, Write this down, for these words are trustworthy and true.

leaderPrimer:
You did not have to do this, and the fact that you said yes matters more than you know. So before you open the first session, sit with me for a while, because this study will only go as deep as you are willing to go first, and the most important preparation is not mastering the material. It is settling your own heart, and being honest about your own hope and your own doubt. The aim of this series is to put the real Christian hope back in front of people, the resurrection of the body and the life of the world to come, in place of the thin clouds-and-harps fantasy most of us inherited, and to do it without flinching from the hard things and without using any of it as a weapon. Notice what the aim is not. It is not to win arguments about the timing of the end. It is not to settle, once and for all, exactly what hell is, because faithful Christians have read the same Scriptures and landed in different places. It is not to make grieving people stop grieving. If anyone leaves this series with their hope smaller, or their grief shamed, or their neighbor consigned to hell more easily, the study failed, however orthodox it sounded.

Two dangers will sit in your room from the first night, and you need to see them before they arrive. The first is the danger of the third session, on hell. The temptation there runs in two opposite directions, and you must refuse both. Some in the room will want to gloat, to enjoy the doctrine, to relish the damnation of people they dislike, and you must shut that down with everything in you, gently but completely, because Jesus reserved his hottest words for exactly those people. Others in the room will want to flinch, to edit the warnings of Jesus out of the faith because they are uncomfortable, and you must not let them do that either, because a Christianity that keeps the comfort of Christ and throws away his warnings has kept a fragment and lost the Lord. The whole posture of that session, and your whole posture as you lead it, is this. Never gloat. Never flinch. Lay the historic views out at full strength, the traditional eternal conscious punishment, the conditionalist view, and the reach of universalism, and let people wrestle before God rather than before a caricature. Say plainly that the first two are held within orthodoxy by serious believers, and that you are not going to settle it for them in five weeks. If a skeptic is in the room, and Bell was once that skeptic, take the objection at full weight. The disproportion between a finite life and an infinite penalty is the hardest thing in the faith, and a leader who pretends it is easy will lose the very people who most need to stay in the conversation.

The second danger is the fourth session, on death and grief, because there will be fresh grief in your room and you may not know it. Someone buried a spouse this year. Someone is watching a parent fade. Someone lost a child and has never been able to say so in church. When you open the subject of the dead in Christ, you are touching the rawest wound many people carry, and the room must be a place where that wound can be uncovered without being fixed. Do not let the group rush to comfort. Do not let anyone slap a verse on a grieving person to make the tears stop. The single most important thing you can model is what Paul actually said, which is not do not grieve, but do not grieve as those who have no hope. Real grief is allowed. Full tears are allowed. The faith does not ask people to perform a peace they do not feel at a graveside. It asks them to grieve toward a morning. Hold those two together, grief and hope, and do not let the group drop either one. If someone weeps, let them weep. Thank them for their honesty. Do not tidy it up.

Now the part it would be easiest to skip, your own heart. You cannot lead people toward a hope you have not let do its work in you. If you walk in as the one who has it all figured out, dispensing certainties about the afterlife to the confused, you have already failed, because Bell does not stand there and neither can you. He came to faith out of atheism, and hell was the thing he held hardest against God, and he will tell you he has not solved it, only that he met the One who warned of the cliff and then went over it himself. He was raised without a father and has buried people he loved, and he knows the particular ache of grieving a presence he barely had. He has wanted to flee a world that breaks his heart, and he has wanted, in his tired and faithless hours, to give up the horizon altogether. He writes from inside the longing and the doubt and the grief, and the power of this whole series depends on you doing the same. So before session one, find your own doubt and your own grief and your own longing, and name them honestly. What do you actually believe happens when you die. What loss are you carrying. Where has your hope gone thin. Do not hide it. The leader who can say I do not have this all figured out either, but here is the One I trust, can lead a room of doubters and grievers without contempt and without distance.

You will face several kinds of people. The first is the lifelong believer who has never once examined the clouds-and-harps picture and may be startled, even unsettled, to hear that the Bible promises a resurrected body on a renewed earth rather than a soul in the sky. Do not mock the picture they inherited. Help them trade it for the larger one gently, and give them time, because a hope held since childhood does not get replaced in an evening. The second is the griever, raw and recent, for whom the fourth session is not theology but survival. Handle them like the wounded they are. The third is the skeptic, perhaps invited, perhaps a believer with honest doubts about hell or about the whole idea of an afterlife, who needs to find that this room will take the hardest questions seriously rather than scolding them for asking. Bell was that skeptic. Welcome the questions. The fourth is the one who wants to argue the timetable, the charts and the sequences, and your job is to keep gently turning the room back from speculation to the hope itself, because the study is about the country we are going to, not the schedule of the trip.

One more practical word before the charge. Watch the clock and the temperature together, especially in sessions three and four, which can go to deep and painful and contested places. You are not aiming to resolve the doctrine of hell in the room, and you are not aiming to leave a grieving person exposed and raw at the end of the night. When something heavy surfaces, slow your own voice, do not let the group swarm it, and when it is time, move gently toward the practice, the reflection, and the prayer, because none of this finally lands as an idea discussed. It lands as a hope carried, or a grief brought, toward Christ. Trust the closing prayer to do work the discussion cannot. End every session there, even when nothing felt resolved, because the last things do not resolve on a schedule and a room sent out toward Jesus is better off than a room sent out with a tidy chart. Resist the urge to tie a bow, especially on hell. The unresolved ending is not a failure. It is the honest shape of a hope held this side of the morning.

Here is your charge. You are not the one who has seen the country. You are a fellow traveler who happens to be holding the readings, pointing everyone, yourself first, toward the One who has been to the far side of the grave and came back with the scars. Lead like that. Refuse every chance to gloat about hell or to flinch from it. Refuse every chance to shame a grieving person or to shrink the hope to a postcard. Let the weight of these sessions rest on you first and most honestly, and when you yourself doubt, or grieve, or ache for a morning you cannot see, say so out loud, because your honesty will preach louder than your competence ever could. The goal is not a room that has the afterlife figured out. The goal is a room full of people, you first, who have traded a thin hope for a solid one, who can grieve toward a morning, who refuse both the bunker and the chaplaincy, and who are learning to live the long defeat with their eyes on the dawn. Go gently. Go honestly. Go first.

faq.q: Is this study going to give me a chart of the end times, the rapture, the millennium, all of it?
faq.a: No, and that is deliberate. This study is about the country we are going to, not the schedule of the trip. It deals with the great shared hope of the whole church, the resurrection of the body, the new heavens and new earth, the intermediate state, and the honest question of hell, the things Christians across the centuries have confessed together. It does not take sides on the timing debates that divide believers, the sequences and charts and competing systems, because those are secondary to the hope itself and arguing them tends to crowd out the very thing the study is for. If you came for a timetable, you will be disappointed. If you came to recover a solid hope, you are in the right place.

faq.q: Does the study think heaven is clouds and harps and floating souls?
faq.a: The opposite, and the first session is built to clear that picture away. The clouds-and-harps heaven, a disembodied soul drifting in the sky forever, is not the Christian hope but a fragment mistaken for the whole, stitched together from paintings and funeral sentiment and traceable more to Plato than to Scripture. The Bible promises resurrection, bodies raised on a renewed earth, God coming down to dwell with his people, the New Jerusalem descending. The movement of the Christian hope is downward and earthward, God making his home with us, not souls escaping upward and away. The study, following N.T. Wright among others, works to trade the postcard for the real country, which is larger, stranger, and far more physical than most of us were taught.

faq.q: Is the resurrection of the body really necessary, or can I just believe my soul goes to heaven?
faq.a: The resurrection of the body is the Christian hope, not an optional extra, and the second session makes the case the way Paul did. In First Corinthians 15 Paul says that if Christ has not been raised, bodily, your faith is worthless, and he offers no fallback to a surviving soul. The faith is resurrection or it is nothing. The immortality of the soul, the assumption that we simply float on somewhere forever, is closer to the Greek philosophy of Plato than to Scripture, which promises something only God can do, the raising of the dead. Your soul being with the Lord when you die is real and good, but it is the corridor, not the room. The destination is your body raised, transformed and imperishable, on a healed earth.

faq.q: Does this study believe in hell, and which view does it teach?
faq.a: It believes the question of hell is real and must be faced honestly, and it deliberately does not force one view on you. The third session lays out three historic positions each at full strength. The traditional view of eternal conscious punishment, the majority across church history, held by Augustine and the Reformers and defended in our time by writers like J.I. Packer and Robert Peterson, grounded in the warnings of Jesus himself. The conditionalist or annihilationist view, held tentatively by John Stott and argued by Edward Fudge, that the finally lost are judged and then cease to be. And universalism, which the study takes seriously for the beauty of its hope but judges to overreach. The study holds the first two within orthodoxy and refuses to settle it for you in five weeks. What it insists on is the posture, never gloat about hell and never flinch from it.

faq.q: How can a loving God send anyone to hell? That is the thing I cannot get past.
faq.a: Then you are in good company, because James Bell came to faith out of atheism and hell was the single thing he held hardest against God, and he will not pretend now that he has made it easy. The third session states the objection at full weight, the disproportion between a finite life and an infinite penalty, and refuses to wave it away. It then lays out how serious Christians have answered, the traditional view that God honors human freedom all the way down and will not drag into his presence those who spent a life refusing it, and the conditionalist view that the lost are judged and then perish rather than suffering endlessly. The study does not hand you a tidy solution. What it offers is that the One who warns of the dark is the same One who walked into it himself, on the cross, and came out with the scars, which means the Judge can be trusted even where the answer is withheld.

faq.q: What does the Bible actually say happens the moment I die?
faq.a: More than we usually notice and less than we wish, and the fourth session walks through it carefully. The consistent witness is that those who die in Christ are immediately and consciously with the Lord. Paul says to be absent from the body is to be present with the Lord, and calls it far better. Jesus tells the dying thief, today you will be with me in paradise. So the dead in Christ are not unconscious and not gone, they are home, at rest, safe. But this is the intermediate state, the corridor and not the room. They are not yet raised, their bodies are still in the ground, and they wait, content but expectant, for the resurrection morning when body and soul are rejoined on the new earth. Even the faithful dead, the study notes, are leaning forward toward the trumpet.

faq.q: My grief is overwhelming. Does my sorrow mean my faith is too weak?
faq.a: No, and the fourth session cuts that shame off at the root. Paul does not tell grieving Christians not to grieve. He tells them not to grieve as those who have no hope, which means Christian grief is real grief, full weight, honest tears, because death is a genuine wound and the separation is real. Hope does not cancel the grief, it changes its color. You weep, but at a train platform and not a tomb, for someone gone ahead and not gone out. Bell, who was raised without a father and has buried people he loved, will not pretend the doctrine removes the pain. Lewis wrote A Grief Observed in raw anguish after his wife died and his faith did not spare him the sorrow, it carried him through it. Your grief is love with nowhere to put itself yet, not a failure of belief.

faq.q: Is not all this talk of heaven just escapism that makes Christians useless on earth?
faq.a: It is a fair charge against a false version of the hope, and the study agrees with the charge against that version while showing it gets the true hope backwards. The fifth session names the eschatology of the bunker, the believer who will not plant trees because the orchard is doomed, and rejects it, because the second session showed the earth is going to be healed and not discarded. A hope of healing does not produce people who abandon the patient, it produces people who fight for it. The believer who knows his body will be raised cannot despise his body now, and people who know the earth will be made new cannot treat it as a dumpster. Rightly understood, the hope of resurrection does not pull you off the earth. It plants you in it, freed from despair, able to labor at a losing battle because you know who finally wins.

faq.q: What is the long defeat, and why does the study end there?
faq.a: The long defeat is a phrase from Tolkien for the Christian experience of history as a fighting retreat, the slow erosion, the cause that loses ground, the body that fails, the world that does not get visibly better on our watch. The study ends there, in the fifth session, because that is honestly where most of us live, and a hope that cannot speak into the long defeat is no use. Against it the study sets what Tolkien called eucatastrophe, the good catastrophe, the sudden joyous turn when all seemed lost, of which the resurrection is the first and the guarantee. Lewis reached for the same thing at the end of Narnia, the morning when the great story begins and every chapter is better than the one before. The point is that we live the long defeat with the courage of people who have read the last page and know it ends with a morning.

faq.q: Why does the study lean on N.T. Wright, Lewis, and Tolkien so much?
faq.a: Because each of them recovered something the modern church had let go thin. N.T. Wright, especially in Surprised by Hope, has spent a career waking the church from the sleep of imagining heaven as a disembodied escape and recovering the biblical hope of resurrection and new creation, which anchors the first two sessions. C.S. Lewis, in The Great Divorce and A Grief Observed and the close of Narnia, gave the church images for the solidity of the world to come, the freedom of the damned who lock the door from the inside, and the honesty of grief held alongside hope. Tolkien gave us the long defeat and eucatastrophe, the shape of a hope that endures the dark and aches rightly for the morning. They are witnesses, not the source, the source is Scripture, but they taught a generation to feel the hope and not only to assent to it.

faq.q: I am a skeptic. Is not the afterlife just wishful thinking, a comfort for people afraid to die?
faq.a: It is a fair suspicion, and the study tries to earn the right to answer it by refusing the cheap version of exactly that. James Bell was an atheist, and he will not sell you a soft comfort he himself could not have believed. The study does not promise that this world is fine and you will float away from it. It faces hell as the hardest objection there is, takes the disproportion seriously, and refuses to pretend the doctrine is easy. It grounds the hope not in a feeling but in a historical claim, an empty tomb and a body that was seen and touched and ate, which is a falsifiable thing rather than a warm wish. What it finally offers is not a denial of the dark but the claim that Someone has been to the far side of it and come back. You can weigh that claim. The study does not ask you to pretend.

faq.q: How do I lead this if I have my own doubts about the afterlife and my own grief?
faq.a: Your doubt and your grief are not disqualifications. They may be your best qualification. The study is built to be led by a fellow traveler, not by someone who has seen the country and returned with a map, and every discussion question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than advice, so you are not improvising. Your honesty about your own questions, especially about hell, and your own losses can be the very thing that lets others stop performing a certainty they do not feel. What you need is to refuse to gloat about hell or to flinch from it, to keep the room safe for the grieving and the doubting, to trade the thin picture of heaven for the solid one gently, and to point everyone, yourself first, toward the One who has the scars. Read the leader primer, settle your own heart, and trust the material.

timeline.event: The early books of the Hebrew Scriptures ground the hope in the goodness of the created order, declaring that God made the material world and called it very good, the conviction against which any picture of salvation as escape from the body must finally break.

Isaiah proclaims that God will create new heavens and a new earth and that he will swallow up death forever and wipe away tears from all faces, planting the hope of a renewed creation centuries before John sees the same vision in Revelation.

Plato teaches that the body is a prison of the soul and that the philosopher's hope is the soul's escape from the flesh, the idea that later seeps into the church and produces the disembodied clouds-and-harps picture the Bible never taught.

The hope of bodily resurrection takes clear shape in later Jewish writing, including the book of Daniel's promise that many who sleep in the dust will awake, so that by the first century the resurrection of the dead is a settled hope among the Pharisees.

Jesus is crucified, buried, and on the third day raised bodily, seen and touched and eating fish to prove he is not a ghost, the empty tomb becoming the firstfruits and guarantee of the resurrection hope of the whole church.

Paul writes First Corinthians 15, staking the entire faith on the bodily resurrection, declaring that if Christ has not been raised the faith is worthless, and describing the resurrection body as a seed sown perishable and raised imperishable.

John records the Revelation, seeing a new heaven and a new earth and the holy city coming down from God, the dwelling of God with man, death and mourning and pain passing away, and the One on the throne declaring he is making all things new.

Origen advances a form of the hope that all will finally be restored to God, the early Christian root of universalism, a position the church would contest and at points condemn yet which would recur across the centuries.
Augustine defends the eternal conscious punishment of the lost in The City of God, shaping the view that would become dominant in the Western church for more than a thousand years.

Dante completes his great poem of the afterlife, fixing in the Western imagination a vivid and elaborate picture of hell, purgatory, and paradise that would shape, for better and worse, how generations pictured the life to come.

C. S. Lewis publishes The Great Divorce, picturing the solidity of heaven against the thinness of the damned who cling freely to their misery, and the door of hell locked from the inside, a humane account of the traditional view.

J. R. R. Tolkien develops, in his essay On Fairy-Stories, the idea of eucatastrophe, the sudden joyous turn when all seems lost, and names the Resurrection the eucatastrophe of the whole human story, giving the church a word for its hope.

C. S. Lewis publishes A Grief Observed after the death of his wife, refusing to tidy up his anguish, modeling a Christian grief that is fully honest and yet held within a solid hope, the very posture the fourth session asks of the room.

Edward Fudge publishes The Fire That Consumes, the most sustained modern biblical case for the conditionalist view of final punishment, prompting a renewed and serious evangelical debate over the nature of hell.

John Stott, in a published dialogue, confesses that he leans tentatively toward conditionalism, lending the weight of one of evangelicalism's most respected figures to the view that the lost finally perish rather than suffer endlessly.

N. T. Wright publishes Surprised by Hope, pressing the church to recover the bodily resurrection and the renewal of creation as the true Christian hope, and to abandon the disembodied escape that had replaced it in the popular imagination.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome. Thank you for being here, and thank you for being willing to look at the hardest and largest things there are, what happens when we die and what God is finally doing with the world. Before we start, three things. First, this is a safe room. You can bring your doubt here. You can say I am not sure I believe any of this here. You can bring your grief here, fresh or old, and no one will rush to fix you or tie a bow on your sorrow. Second, this study takes the hard things seriously, the question of hell most of all, and it will never gloat about it and never flinch from it. Faithful Christians have landed in different places on some of this, and we are not here to win arguments but to recover a solid hope. Third, the writer puts himself inside all of this, and so will I. He came to faith out of atheism, and hell was the thing he held hardest against God. He was raised without a father and has buried people he loved. We are not standing over the doubters and the grieving from a safe distance. We are the doubters and the grieving. Tonight we are looking at this together: ________. Let me read our key passage, and then we will sit with it before we say anything else. There are no wrong answers in the first five minutes, only honest ones.
facilitatorScript.transition: We have looked hard at what the passage says. Now let us bring it home, off the page and into the lives we are actually living, into the long defeat and the fresh grief and the ordinary Tuesday, because that is where this hope either matters or it does not.
facilitatorScript.close: We are going to stop there, even though it is not all resolved, because the last things do not resolve on a schedule and pretending otherwise would be a lie. Carry the weight of this toward Jesus this week rather than carrying it alone. Try the practice. Sit with the reflection questions on your own. And if tonight has stirred up grief or doubt that is too heavy to carry by yourself, please tell someone, because this is exactly what the body of Christ is for. Let me pray for us before we go. Thank you for the honesty it took to be in this room.

cadences.name: The full study (8 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Orientation. Read the summary together, set the ground rules about safety, doubt, and grief, and walk session 1's opening questions slowly. Name plainly that hell will be handled without gloating and without flinching, and that grief will be honored.
Week 2: Session 1, The Wrong Picture, full discussion and practice, with time on where our inherited picture of heaven came from.
Week 3: Session 2, The Resurrection of the Body, with extended time on N.T. Wright's life after life-after-death and the redemption of creation.
Week 4: Session 3, Hell, Honestly, part one, stating the objection at full weight and laying out the traditional view of eternal conscious punishment.
Week 5: Session 3 continued, the conditionalist view and where universalism overreaches, holding all three at full strength, plus practice and prayer.
Week 6: Session 4, The Dead in Christ, the intermediate state and the communion of saints, with gentle, unhurried space for grief.
Week 7: Session 5, The Long Defeat and the Final Morning, the two wrong answers and the courage the true hope produces.
Week 8: Integration. Revisit all five practices, the scripture index, and what each person is carrying toward Christ, with space for anyone wrestling with grief or doubt to be prayed for.

cadences.name: The intensive (4 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Sessions 1 and 2 together, the wrong picture cleared away and the resurrection of the body recovered.
Week 2: Session 3, Hell, Honestly, with extended time so all three views can be laid out fairly and the objection taken at full weight.
Week 3: Session 4, The Dead in Christ, the intermediate state, the communion of saints, and grief held with hope.
Week 4: Session 5, The Long Defeat and the Final Morning, plus a short integration close on living now in light of then.

cadences.name: As written (5 weeks)
plan: Week 2: Session 2, The Resurrection of the Body.
Week 4: Session 4, The Dead in Christ.
Week 5: Session 5, The Long Defeat and the Final Morning.

bibliography.title: Surprised by Hope: Rethinking Heaven, the Resurrection, and the Mission of the Church
bibliography.author: N. T. Wright
bibliography.note: The central modern recovery of the bodily resurrection and the renewal of creation against the disembodied escape, and the source of the phrase life after life-after-death. The spine of sessions 1 and 2.

bibliography.title: The Great Divorce
bibliography.author: C. S. Lewis
bibliography.note: Pictures the solidity of heaven against the thinness of the damned who lock the door from the inside, a humane imagining of the traditional view of hell. Anchors sessions 1 and 3.

bibliography.title: A Grief Observed
bibliography.author: C. S. Lewis
bibliography.note: Lewis's raw, untidied record of grief after his wife's death, modeling sorrow held honestly within a solid hope. The pastoral spine of session 4.

bibliography.title: The Fire That Consumes: A Biblical and Historical Study of the Doctrine of Final Punishment
bibliography.author: Edward Fudge
bibliography.note: The most sustained modern biblical case for the conditionalist view of hell. Used in session 3 to present that position at full strength. Leader to confirm specific claims before attributing them to Bell.

bibliography.title: Hell Under Fire: Modern Scholarship Reinvents Eternal Punishment
bibliography.author: Robert A. Peterson and others
bibliography.note: A defense of the traditional view of eternal conscious punishment engaging the modern debate. Used in session 3 to present the historic position at full strength. Leader to confirm specifics before pressing them as settled.

bibliography.title: The Lord of the Rings and On Fairy-Stories
bibliography.author: J. R. R. Tolkien
bibliography.note: The source of the long defeat and of eucatastrophe, the sudden joyous turn that Tolkien names the shape of the Resurrection. Anchors session 5. Leader to confirm exact wording before quoting.

bibliography.title: The Last Battle
bibliography.author: C. S. Lewis
bibliography.note: The close of the Narnia stories, with its image of death as the end of the holidays and the beginning of a story in which every chapter is better than the one before. Supports session 5.

bibliography.title: Heaven
bibliography.author: Randy Alcorn
bibliography.note: A long, detailed treatment of the new earth and the physicality of the resurrection hope, useful for readers who want to dwell on the concreteness of the world to come. Leader to confirm before stating its claims as the study's own position, offered as a supporting voice for sessions 1 and 2.

bibliography.title: The City of God
bibliography.author: Augustine of Hippo
bibliography.note: The classic source of the Western defense of eternal conscious punishment and a sweeping vision of the two cities and the end of history. Background for session 3 and the timeline.

bibliography.title: Knowing God
bibliography.author: J. I. Packer
bibliography.note: Packer's writing represents the careful, pastoral defense of the historic doctrines, including the traditional view of judgment. Background for the historic position in session 3. Leader to confirm specific claims before attributing them to Bell.

bibliography.title: The Divine Comedy
bibliography.author: Dante Alighieri
bibliography.note: The great poem that fixed a vivid picture of the afterlife in the Western imagination, for better and worse. Useful background for session 1 on how our pictures of the life to come were formed. Offered as historical context, not doctrine.

bibliography.title: Evangelical Essentials, the dialogue containing his comments on final punishment
bibliography.author: John Stott with David Edwards
bibliography.note: The published dialogue in which Stott tentatively confesses a leaning toward conditionalism, lending weight to that view's place within evangelical orthodoxy. Used in session 3. Leader to confirm the exact wording before pressing it.

furtherReading: Surprised by Hope, N. T. Wright, for readers who want to sit longer with the bodily resurrection and the renewal of creation that anchor the first two sessions.
The Great Divorce, C. S. Lewis, for those who want a humane and imaginative account of heaven, hell, and the freedom of the soul that locks its own door.
A Grief Observed, C. S. Lewis, for anyone walking through fresh grief who needs to see sorrow held honestly within a hope that does not tidy it up.

The Fire That Consumes, Edward Fudge, for readers who want the conditionalist case made at length and biblically, read alongside a strong defense of the traditional view, leader to confirm specific claims.

Hell Under Fire, Robert Peterson and others, for those who want the historic view of eternal conscious punishment defended carefully in the modern debate, so both serious positions are heard at full strength.

glossary.definition: The Christian hope that the dead will be raised bodily, the same self transformed and made imperishable, not a disembodied soul but a renewed physical person on a renewed earth, patterned on the risen Christ who was seen and touched and ate.

The biblical promise that God will not discard the creation but heal it, the present world set free from decay and made new, with the dwelling of God come down to be among his people, as Isaiah foresaw and John saw in Revelation.

N. T. Wright's phrase for the fuller hope beyond the soul's presence with Christ at death, namely the bodily resurrection on the new earth, the room beyond the corridor, the destination the intermediate state is waiting for.

The condition of the dead in Christ between death and the resurrection, consciously present with the Lord, at rest and safe, yet not yet raised, awaiting the resurrection morning when body and soul are rejoined. The corridor, not the room.

The confession that the church is not divided by death but is one body in Christ, the living and the faithful dead joined together in him, those we have buried more deeply united to the Head of the body than ever, ahead of us on the same road.

The traditional and historically majority view of hell, that the finally lost are consciously and everlastingly separated from God, grounded in the warnings of Jesus and defended by Augustine, the Reformers, and modern writers such as J. I. Packer and Robert Peterson.

Also called annihilationism, the view that immortality is a gift given to the redeemed rather than an automatic possession, and that the finally unrepentant are judged and then cease to exist. Held tentatively by John Stott and argued by Edward Fudge.

The hope that all will finally be saved, taken seriously in this study for the beauty of its impulse, the longing that none be lost, yet judged to overreach because it must either empty the warnings of Jesus or deny the freedom that love requires.

J. R. R. Tolkien's word for the sudden joyous turn at the darkest moment of a story, the unexpected deliverance that pierces sorrow with a sharp joy. Tolkien named the Resurrection the eucatastrophe of the whole human story.

Tolkien's phrase for the Christian experience of history as a fighting retreat, the slow erosion, the cause that loses ground, lived with courage because beneath and beyond it lies the final morning the Resurrection guarantees.
Paul's image for the resurrection of Christ as the first sheaf of a harvest, the down payment and guarantee that the rest of the field, the bodily raising of all who are his, is certain to follow.

The Greek philosophical tradition that treats the body as a prison and the soul's escape from the flesh as salvation, the borrowed idea that produced the disembodied clouds-and-harps picture of heaven the Bible never taught.

The phrase from Revelation for the final fate of the lost, read by the conditionalist as a real and final ceasing and by the traditional view as a conscious and unending separation, one of the contested texts in the doctrine of hell.
